description: Width tiers for Geography Year 8 (ACARA v9) — all 15 descriptors across K and S strands
subject: Geography

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest engagement that satisfies the descriptor's command term. For K-strand (Knowledge and Understanding), minimum is the fewest phenomena or contexts in which the concept is genuinely explained. For S-strand (Skills), minimum is the narrowest single task context in which the skill is demonstrably applied. Minimum is not what is easy — it is what the command term requires.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope grounded in the most common elaboration cases. Reflects what a well-taught class would have engaged with. Does not require every elaboration to be covered, but requires the descriptor's scope and spirit to be met.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, cultural contexts, or task types — not harder versions of the same context. Includes First Nations directions where elaborations indicate them. Each wider item is a concrete direction, not a vague suggestion.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are used as source data for grounding typical_width and identifying the range of phenomena or contexts the descriptor is intended to cover. First Nations elaborations are treated as default wider directions. Elaborations are not a checklist — some are merged where they represent variants of the same phenomenon.

AC9HG8K01.minimum_width: Explain one geomorphological process (e.g. folding, erosion, or volcanism) and the landform it produces, using a named example at one scale.
AC9HG8K01.typical_width: Explain the diversity of landscape types (wetlands, grasslands, forests, deserts) and how tectonic, volcanic, fold, fault, weathering (chemical and physical) and erosion/transportation/deposition processes produce different landforms. Apply process explanations to named examples at national and local scales, distinguishing the effects of rock type on landform character.
wider: Compare the role of endogenic (internal) vs exogenic (surface) processes in producing a selected landscape, examining how both contribute to its current form over geological time
Investigate how the same surface process (e.g. water erosion) produces dramatically different landforms depending on rock type, climate and scale
Examine how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples explain landform formation through Dreaming stories and what geographic knowledge these narratives encode
Explore how landscape distribution patterns at the global scale correlate with tectonic settings (e.g. volcanic arcs, rift zones, shield regions)
elaborations: explaining the diversity of landscapes, such as wetlands, grasslands, forests, cold and hot deserts, and landforms at the national scale; for example, mountains – Himalayan Mountains, Nepal; grasslands – the Steppe, central Asia; forests – Daintree, Australia; cold deserts – Gobi, China

explaining how tectonics, volcanism, folding, faulting, chemical weathering and physical weathering such as erosion, transportation and deposition shape places; for example, folding – MacDonnell Ranges, Northern Territory, Australia; faulting – Great Sumatran Fault (Semangko Fault), Indonesia; volcanism – Krakatoa, Indonesia

explaining the effects of rock type on a selected landform at the local scale; such as Fraser Island, Queensland or Twelve Apostles, Victoria; for example, sedimentary – igneous and metamorphic; chemical weathering – oxidation and solution; physical weathering – exfoliation and frost wedging

explaining the effects of erosion, transportation and deposition of water and wind on a selected landform at the local scale; for example, Fraser Island, Queensland, formed by wind, waves and ocean currents; the Twelve Apostles, Victoria, formed by erosion, tides and ocean currents

AC9HG8K02.minimum_width: Locate and name at least three distinctive Australian landscapes or significant landforms on a map and describe their distribution. Explain the significance of one landform to a First Nations Australian community.
AC9HG8K02.typical_width: Represent the distribution of Australia's distinctive landscapes (deserts in Central Australia, tropical rainforests in the north) and significant landforms (Uluru, Blue Mountains) on a map, describing what makes selected landscapes iconic. Compare the distribution of Australian landscapes with those of another country. Explain the significance of a landform important to First Nations Australians including its name, meaning and cultural/spiritual significance.
wider: Investigate how First Nations place names encode geographic and environmental knowledge about landscapes — examining specific examples from different Country
Compare how the same place (e.g. Uluru-Kata Tjuta) is understood differently by First Nations communities, mainstream tourism and geomorphological science
Examine how native title, land rights and World Heritage listing intersect with the recognition of First Nations connections to iconic Australian landscapes
elaborations: representing the distribution of Australian distinctive landscapes, such as the deserts in Central Australia, and significant landforms, such as Uluru in Central Australia
locating iconic landscapes and landforms in Australia on a map and describing what makes them iconic

comparing the distribution of Australia's distinctive landscapes with distinctive landscapes in another country; for example, grasslands in Arnhem Land in northern Australia compared to grasslands in Mongolia; tropical rainforests in northern Australia compared to forests in Laos and Cambodia

explaining the significance of a landform important to First Nations Australians; for example, the names, meanings and significance of the Three Sisters in the Blue Mountains, New South Wales; Budj Bim cultural landscape within Gunditjmara Country; Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park in Northern Territory

AC9HG8K03.minimum_width: Explain at least two types of value (spiritual, aesthetic, cultural) that landscapes hold for people, with one example each. Explain the multilayered meanings of one landscape or landform for First Nations Australians.
AC9HG8K03.typical_width: Explain the spiritual, aesthetic and cultural value of landscapes for people using multiple cultural contexts (e.g. Mt Fuji and Yellow Mountains for Japanese and Chinese contexts; tourism at Uluru). Examine how Dreaming stories and Torres Strait Islander Creation stories give meaning to Country/Place, including the multilayered material, cultural and spiritual wellbeing dimensions of First Nations relationships to landscapes.
wider: Examine how Dreaming stories encode geographic knowledge — seasonal indicators, species distributions, water sources — alongside spiritual meaning, and what this reveals about First Nations environmental understanding
Compare how the spiritual significance of a landscape is expressed and transmitted differently across First Nations communities, examining the role of ceremony, oral tradition and land management
Investigate how tourism industries commodify aesthetic landscape value and what tensions this creates for the spiritual and cultural values held by First Nations Australians
Explore the formation of a significant landform and connect this to the Dreaming or Creation story associated with it, examining how physical and cultural knowledge coexist
elaborations: identifying the ways people value significant landscapes in Japan and China, such as Mt Fuji and the Yellow Mountains respectively, and describing what makes them important
analysing the role of landforms and landscapes in tourism; for example, Uluru in Australia or the Himalayas in Nepal
examining how Aboriginal Dreaming stories and Torres Strait Islander Creation stories give meaning to Country/Place
discussing the meaning of the stories that describe First Nations Australians' special connection to Country/Place
discussing the multilayered meanings (material, cultural and spiritual wellbeing) associated with landscapes and significant landforms for First Nations Australians
explaining the formation of a landform with reference to the special connections First Nations Australians have to Country/Place

AC9HG8K04.minimum_width: Explain the interconnections between one human activity and a geomorphological process, identifying the environmental effects. Identify one way that landscapes are managed.
AC9HG8K04.typical_width: Explain the interconnections between multiple human activities (tourism overuse, land clearing, mining, urban development, river regulation) and geomorphological processes, identifying their effects on landscape quality. Explain the contribution of First Nations Australian knowledges to the use and management of distinctive landscapes.
wider: Investigate a specific case study in depth — the Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River or dams on the Murray-Darling system — tracing the chain of interconnections from river regulation through to downstream landscape and ecological effects
Compare government-led and First Nations-led landscape management approaches for the same landscape, examining what each prioritises and how outcomes differ
Examine how land clearing for agricultural production (e.g. palm oil in Indonesia and Malaysia) creates interconnections that operate across local, national and global scales
elaborations: identifying the interconnections and effects of erosion and sedimentation produced by human activities on the quality of the environment; for example, the effects of overuse of tourist tracks in bushland or the effects of land-clearing for the production of palm oil in Indonesia and Malaysia

explaining the interconnections and effects of mining, quarrying and urban development on the quality of the environment; for example, the interconnections of the quality of the environment and uranium mining in Kakadu, urban development in Singapore or the extension of land area in Tokyo Bay

explaining the effects of river regulation, including dams, locks, channel straightening and drains, on the quality of riverine and wetland environments; for example, the Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River in China, or dams and weirs on the Murray–Darling River system

identifying the contribution of the knowledges of First Nations Australians to the use and management of distinctive landscapes; for example, Indigenous Peoples' Knowledge (IPK) incorporated into modern management of diverse landscapes and landforms such as Kakadu National Park, Uluru, the Great Barrier Reef and the Snowy Mountains

AC9HG8K05.minimum_width: Explain the causes and at least two impacts (environmental, economic or social) of one geomorphological hazard on people, places and environments, using a named case study. Identify one response strategy and its intended effect.
AC9HG8K05.typical_width: Explain the causes of a selected geomorphological hazard (volcanic eruption, earthquake, tsunami, landslide or avalanche), examine its environmental, economic and social impacts at the local scale, and explain how responses based on prevention, mitigation and preparedness reduce harmful effects. Reflect on how human activity has heightened vulnerability.
wider: Compare the impacts of the same hazard type in places with different levels of economic development and infrastructure, examining how vulnerability is unevenly distributed
Investigate how human modifications to the environment (land clearing, coastal development, urban expansion on floodplains) have heightened the impact of geomorphological hazards in specific cases
Examine how early warning systems, community preparedness and governance capacity interact to determine hazard outcomes — using a comparative case study
elaborations: identifying the causes of a geomorphological hazard such as a volcanic eruption, earthquake, tsunami, landslide or avalanche

examining the environmental, economic or social impacts of a hazard at the local scale; for example, where people choose to live; the negative consequences for human wellbeing including loss of industry and unemployment; and lack of infrastructure and resources to prepare and respond to hazards
reflecting on observations of a location where the environment has been altered by human activities to explain how the change has heightened the impact of a hazard
reflecting on the principles of prevention, mitigation and preparedness to explain how the harmful effects of a hazard can be reduced by the implementation of a management strategy

AC9HG8K06.minimum_width: Distinguish urban growth from urbanisation and explain at least two push-pull factors driving population movement. Explain one positive and one negative impact of urbanisation using a country study.
AC9HG8K06.typical_width: Explain the causes of urbanisation including push-pull forces, the growth of megacities and urban corridors, the effects of economic conditions on urban character, and the connections between urbanisation and economic/social opportunities and environmental impacts. Draw on a country study (e.g. USA) throughout.
wider: Compare urbanisation trajectories in a developed country (USA) and a rapidly urbanising developing country, identifying structural differences in causes and pace
Investigate gentrification as an economic-urban process in a specific Australian city, examining causes and the differential effects on existing residents
Examine how the growth of megacities creates problems of scale not present in large cities — using a specific megacity case study to trace infrastructure, environmental and governance challenges
elaborations: explaining the difference between urban growth and urbanisation, and how push-pull forces contribute to internal and international population movements and increase the size of urban areas

distinguishing between large cities and the rise of megacities at the national scale, including the growth of large capital cities in Australia, Los Angeles as a megacity, or Boston – Washington as an urban corridor in the United States of America

explaining how changes in economic conditions affect the characteristics of urban places, including population growth in a tourist community in coastal New South Wales such as Byron Bay, population decline in a regional area such as Carnarvon Shire, or old industrial areas evolving into areas of urban renewal, and urban villages in Green Square and Barangaroo, Sydney
explaining the connections between urbanisation and economic and social opportunities; for example, the location of universities, sporting stadiums or parliaments in capital cities
explaining how urbanisation can positively or negatively affect the quality of the environment; for example, increases in carbon emissions or increases in water consumption

AC9HG8K07.minimum_width: Represent the distribution of urban settlements in Australia and another country on a map and describe at least two differences in the pattern. Explain at least two causes of urban concentration in Australia.
AC9HG8K07.typical_width: Represent and compare urban settlement distribution in Australia and the USA, identifying similarities and differences. Examine the causes of urban concentration in Australia (history, migration, export economy, environmental constraints, transport networks). Interpret the relationship between population density and proximity to urban centres. Examine the effects of urban concentration including environmental and social impacts.
wider: Analyse census data to map population density gradients around a major Australian city, examining where density drops most steeply and connecting this to transport infrastructure
Compare how Australia's unique urban concentration pattern (coastal capital cities) reflects geographic and historical causes that differ from countries with more dispersed settlement
Investigate how remote and regional communities experience the inverse of urban concentration — declining services, population loss — as a consequence of the same forces driving urban growth
elaborations: representing the location of urban settlements in Australia and the United States of America, identifying similarities and differences in the distribution

examining the causes of urban concentration in Australia; for example, the history of European settlement, migration, the export orientation of the economy, the centralisation of state governments, environmental constraints and the shape of transportation networks

examining the effects of urban concentration in a country other than Australia; for example, the decline in biodiversity and increase in waste, the increase in carbon emissions leading to a large carbon footprint, or the decline in access to adequate clean water and the development of slums

interpreting and explaining the relationship between population density and proximity to urban centres at the national scale; for example, higher population density towards the urban central business district (CBD) as a centre of employment, education, culture and government, such as in Brisbane, and declining towards the rural-urban fringe (core and periphery)

AC9HG8K08.minimum_width: Explain at least two types of migration (e.g. permanent, forced, circular) and at least two reasons driving migration in Australia or China. Explain one effect of migration on a place of origin or destination.
AC9HG8K08.typical_width: Explain the main types and patterns of internal and international migration. Explain the reasons for migration in Australia (mining development, chain migration, employment) and China (internal migration and urban concentration). Interpret population data to describe the relationship between migration and urban concentration in at least one country. Examine how migration affects cultural diversity in destination places.
wider: Compare the causes and effects of internal migration in China with international migration into Australia, examining how scale, policy and economic context differ
Investigate the brain drain effect — how skilled worker migration affects places of origin in Australia's regions or in source countries for international migration
Examine how climate-driven displacement is emerging as a distinct migration driver, tracing specific cases and their implications for traditional migration typologies
elaborations: identifying and explaining the main types and patterns of internal and international migration, such as permanent migration, temporary labour migration, student migration, forced migration (including refugees, illegal migrants and illegally trafficked people) and circular migration

explaining how mining developments affect employment growth in regions and cities, and influence internal migration in Australia; for example, migration leading to population growth in mining areas such as Pilbara in Western Australia and Bowen Basin in North Queensland

explaining changing influences on migration over time; for example, chain migration related to connection to family, employment, education or health; circular migration involving short-term mobility related to visits to family or for a cultural event
identifying and explaining the patterns of temporary internal migration and permanent internal migration in China and the effects on the places of origin and destination
interpreting population data and describing the relationship between international migration and urban concentration within Australia, and internal migration and urban concentration within China
exploring the connections between the cultural diversity of places and how they are affected by internal and international migration; for example, in Australia or China

AC9HG8K09.minimum_width: Identify one government strategy for managing projected population growth in an Australian urban place and explain at least two implications for sustainability (environmental, economic or social).
AC9HG8K09.typical_width: Examine strategies used by local, state or national governments to manage projected population growth in Australian cities or regional urban centres, identifying implications for environmental, economic and social sustainability and liveability. Consider decentralisation strategies such as Canberra as a case study of planned redistribution.
wider: Compare urban consolidation and decentralisation strategies, evaluating trade-offs for liveability, environmental cost and economic viability in the Australian context
Investigate a specific urban renewal or transit-oriented development project in an Australian city, examining how it addresses sustainability dimensions and how residents have responded
Evaluate the long-term effectiveness of a past urban sustainability strategy using available data on environmental and demographic outcomes
elaborations: examining a strategy used by local, state or national governments to manage projected population growth in one of Australia's cities or regional urban centres, and identifying implications for sustainability (environmental, economic and social factors) and liveability
generating ideas for a strategy for a more balanced distribution of urban population, such as decentralisation, using Canberra as an example

AC9HG8S01.minimum_width: Develop at least one geographical inquiry question for a Y8 phenomenon (geomorphological process or urbanisation challenge) and plan a basic investigation identifying the scale and one data collection approach.
AC9HG8S01.typical_width: Develop questions to investigate why a geographical phenomenon has changed or why a challenge may arise. Plan an investigation at a range of scales using digital planning tools, identifying the scope, scale(s) and methods appropriate to a Y8 context (e.g. geomorphological landform formation at local scale; urbanisation causes and consequences at national scale).
wider: Develop a multi-scale inquiry plan that operates at two different scales (e.g. local and national), explaining how the scale shift changes the evidence required
Evaluate a set of candidate inquiry questions against criteria for productive geographical inquiry, refining the strongest into a question with supporting sub-questions
Design an inquiry plan that incorporates both primary fieldwork and secondary data collection, mapping how each method addresses a different aspect of the inquiry question
elaborations: developing questions to investigate why a geographical phenomenon has changed or why a challenge may arise; for example, "How does urban development affect the sustainability of wetlands?", "Why is biodiversity declining in urban places?"

planning an investigation of a geographical phenomenon or challenge being studied, at a range of scales using digital planning tools; for example, how geomorphological processes produce significant landforms at the local scale, or the causes and consequences of urbanisation at the national scale

AC9HG8S02.minimum_width: Collect data using at least one primary research method and at least two secondary sources, evaluating each secondary source for relevance to the inquiry question.
AC9HG8S02.typical_width: Identify and use appropriate primary research methods including fieldwork and digital tools. Collect secondary research materials using targeted search strategies and evaluate them for relevance and reliability. Identify and respect protocols for First Nations community consultation where relevant. Represent data and information using digital tools in appropriate formats conforming to cartographic conventions.
wider: Compare primary research findings with secondary source findings on the same phenomenon, analysing consistencies and discrepancies and explaining what each source type reveals that the other cannot
Create a multi-layer digital map combining demographic, topographic and qualitative data from primary and secondary sources, justifying cartographic choices
Investigate Indigenous data sovereignty principles and how they shape protocols for geographical research involving First Nations communities and knowledge
elaborations: identifying appropriate primary research methods, including fieldwork, to collect original materials using specialised digital tools; for example, field observations such as sketches or measurements of landscapes or landforms, or digital tools to recreate topographic features of a landform

collecting relevant secondary research materials online using search terms and functions such as "allintitle: geomorphological hazards" or "define: megacities" to identify relevant geographical information

identifying and respecting protocols for consultation with communities of First Nations Australians when organising primary research or fieldwork, such as when discussing Dreaming stories about the formation, meaning and interconnections of Australian landscapes and landforms

evaluating research materials for relevance (for example, "Does the information reflect current thinking about urbanisation?") and reliability (for example, "Who is/are the author/s? Does the author reference other experts in the field?")

comparing findings from primary research methods, including fieldwork, with those from secondary research materials for relevance and reliability; for example, comparing field sketches showing the impact of a geomorphological hazard with newspaper reports on the extent of damage; comparing survey and interview data about people's perception of their suburb with a government report on the impacts of urbanisation

representing relevant and reliable data and information in appropriate formats to combine ideas, using digital tools; for example, creating annotated diagrams to show the changes to a landform over time or using digital mapping tools to show the cultural and demographic diversity of First Nations Australians

representing spatial distributions of different types of geographical phenomena by constructing appropriate maps at different scales that conform to cartographic conventions; for example, constructing a map to show the relationship between landforms such as mountains and landscapes such as deserts, or contrasting the spatial distribution of population in Australia and/or China

AC9HG8S03.minimum_width: Identify at least two similarities and two differences from a geographical data set. Identify and describe one pattern or trend in data, providing a geographic explanation for it.
AC9HG8S03.typical_width: Identify similarities and differences from geographical data including migration source/destination comparisons. Explain patterns and trends using compound graphs or census data across time periods. Infer relationships from primary research data (observations, field sketches, measurements, questionnaires) suggesting possible causes, effects and trends.
wider: Distinguish between correlation and causation in a geographical data set, identifying an example of each and explaining why the distinction matters for geographic conclusions
Analyse data at two different scales for the same phenomenon, examining whether the national pattern holds at the regional level and explaining any discrepancies
Evaluate the reliability and representativeness of a primary data set collected during fieldwork, identifying limitations and how they affect the conclusions that can be drawn
elaborations: identifying similarities and differences from data and information; for example, comparing source and destination of international migration for Australia in 2 different time periods

explaining patterns and trends; for example, comparing compound graphs or census data for different time periods to identify patterns in urban concentration in Australia and the United States of America, or trends in international migration

inferring relationships from data and information collected during primary research; for example, using observations, field sketches, field measurements, questionnaires or interviews to explain the distribution of population in your local area and suggesting possible causes, effects and trends

AC9HG8S04.minimum_width: Draw a conclusion that responds to the inquiry question using at least one geographical concept (place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale or change) as an organiser, citing data evidence.
AC9HG8S04.typical_width: Draw conclusions using at least one geographical concept as an organiser to respond to an inquiry question about landscape value or urbanisation impacts. Explain reasons for decisions and choices made in the analysis, including why particular evidence was weighted or why an impact was judged significant.
wider: Apply two or more geographical concepts simultaneously as conclusion organisers, showing how each concept illuminates a different dimension of the findings
Develop a conclusion that explicitly acknowledges counter-evidence or alternative interpretations, explaining why the primary conclusion is still well-supported
Reflect on how the choice of concept organiser shaped the conclusion reached — what would a different concept (e.g. 'scale' vs 'interconnections') have emphasised or obscured?
elaborations: drawing on the results of an analysis and using at least one of the concepts of place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale or change as an organiser to respond to a question; for example, using research about the value of distinctive landscapes to form conclusions about the influence they have on peoples' lives or an analysis of the distribution of urban settlements to form conclusions about how space is used

explaining reasons for decisions and choices; for example, reflecting on research findings or data analysis of the impacts of geomorphological hazards or urbanisation to identify and explain significant impacts on people, places and environments

AC9HG8S05.minimum_width: Identify or propose one strategy for action related to a Y8 geographical issue, explain at least two potential impacts across different dimensions, and evaluate effectiveness against at least two criteria.
AC9HG8S05.typical_width: Propose individual or collective action related to a geographical issue (landscape degradation, urban sustainability, hazard mitigation), support the proposal with reasons connecting to environmental, economic and social factors, and evaluate the effectiveness of a strategy. Reflect on how personal values influence explanation of potential outcomes.
wider: Compare individual and collective action strategies for the same issue, evaluating what each can realistically achieve at different scales
Develop a detailed impact assessment that distinguishes short-term from long-term consequences and examines how impacts are unevenly distributed across different community groups
Investigate how values and assumptions embedded in a strategy shape what counts as 'effective' — examining a case where different stakeholders assessed the same strategy very differently
elaborations: proposing individual action and supporting the proposal with reasons; for example, reducing waste going to landfill, especially toxic e-waste causing degradation of landscapes, or reducing the large and expanding urban footprint by decreasing the consumption of energy resources as well as eating, working and buying locally

proposing collective action and supporting the proposal with reasons; for example, promoting community awareness of the effects of human–environmental change on significant Australian landforms such as Uluru and the Great Barrier Reef, or encouraging the development of urban and peri-urban agriculture
evaluating the effectiveness of a strategy in relation to environmental, economic and social factors

reflecting on personal values and attitudes and how these influence explanations of potential outcomes; for example, applying sustainable design principles to urban redevelopment projects that provide green, open spaces for citizens

AC9HG8S06.minimum_width: Create a description of a geographical topic using accurate information and at least two geographical terms. Construct an explanation that uses at least one piece of research evidence to support a cause-and-effect claim.
AC9HG8S06.typical_width: Create descriptions that connect the audience to geographical topics using concepts and accurate information. Construct explanations using research findings to support claims about causes and effects of geographical phenomena. Develop responses that use data representations (maps, diagrams, flow maps) to support actions and conclusions.
wider: Develop a multimodal response that integrates written analysis, at least two data representation types (map, graph or diagram), and appropriately referenced sources into a coherent argument
Construct an explanation for two different audiences (e.g. expert geographer vs general public), examining how language, concept use and evidence selection must change
Evaluate the effectiveness of different cartographic and data representation choices for communicating a specific geographic message, justifying the choices made in your own response
elaborations: creating a description that connects the audience to the topic, using geographical concepts and providing accurate information; for example, alleviating the impact of a geological hazard such as volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides and avalanches, or eradicating slums in cities

constructing an explanation, using research findings to support ideas, such as the causes and effects of a geographical phenomenon or challenge, and reinforcing knowledge and understanding of the interconnections between people, places and the environment

developing a response, using representations of data and information to support actions and conclusions, such as a map showing the location of iconic landforms or a flow map showing the international movement of refugees
